        Steps:
        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.
            2.1 create/update dockerfile based on the analysis.

        3. add all changed file to git changes

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a step‑by‑step guide that you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script). It covers everything you asked for: | Step | What to do | Command / File | |------|------------|----------------| | **1** | Clone the repo | `git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git` | | **2** | Analyse & create artefacts | – Dockerfile
– Kubernetes manifests
– GitHub Actions workflow | | **3** | Stage the new files | `git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml` | | **4** | Commit & push | `git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, GitHub Actions"`
`git push origin main` | --- ## 2.1 Dockerfile Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo with the following content: ```dockerfile # Dockerfile # ------------------------------------ # Base image – Node.js 14 on Alpine Linux FROM node:14-alpine # Working directory inside the container WORKDIR /app # Copy package.json & package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache COPY package*.json ./ # Install production dependencies only RUN npm ci --only=production # Copy the rest of the application code COPY . . # Expose the port the app listens on EXPOSE 3000 # Start the application CMD ["node", "app.js"] ``` > **Why this Dockerfile?** > * `node:14-alpine` is lightweight and contains everything needed to run a Node.js app. > * `npm ci` guarantees a reproducible install from `package-lock.json`. > * The app listens on port **3000** (the default for many Express examples). --- ## 2.2 Kubernetes YAMLs Create a directory called `k8s` in the repo root and add two files: ### `k8s/deployment.yaml` ```yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: nodejs-welcome-deployment spec: replicas: 2 selector: matchLabels: app: nodejs-welcome template: metadata: labels: app: nodejs-welcome spec: containers: - name: nodejs-welcome image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest # <-- will be built by GitHub Actions ports: - containerPort: 3000 ``` ### `k8s/service.yaml` ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: nodejs-welcome-service spec: type: LoadBalancer # Change to NodePort/ClusterIP if you prefer selector: app: nodejs-welcome ports: - protocol: TCP port: 80 # External port targetPort: 3000 # Container port ``` > **Tip:** If you’re running locally with Minikube or kind, you can change `type: LoadBalancer` to `NodePort` or `ClusterIP`. --- ## 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow Create the directory `.github/workflows` (if it doesn’t exist) and add a file named `ci.yml`: ```yaml name: CI on: push: branches: - main jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: # Checkout the repo - uses: actions/checkout@v3 # Set up Docker Buildx (multi‑arch support) - name: Set up Docker Buildx uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v2 # Log in to Docker Hub (you’ll need to set secrets in the repo) - name: Login to DockerHub uses: docker/login-action@v2 with: username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }} password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }} # Build the image and push it to Docker Hub - name: Build and push Docker image uses: docker/build-push-action@v3 with: context: . push: true tags: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest # Deploy to Kubernetes (requires a kubeconfig secret) - name: Deploy to Kubernetes uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v1 with: manifests: | k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }} ``` ### What you need to set up in the repo’s **Settings → Secrets** | Secret | Value | |--------|-------| | `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` | Your Docker Hub username | | `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` | A Docker Hub access token (recommended over password) | | `KUBE_CONFIG_DATA` | Base64‑encoded kubeconfig file for the cluster you want to deploy to | > **Why `azure/k8s-deploy`?** > It’s a lightweight action that applies the manifests using `kubectl`. > If you prefer another provider (EKS, GKE, AKS), you can replace it with the appropriate action. --- ## 3. Stage the new files ```bash git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml ``` ## 4. Commit & Push ```bash git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, GitHub Actions workflow" git push origin main ``` --- ### Quick sanity check After pushing, you should see: 1. **GitHub Actions** → “CI” job runs, builds the Docker image, pushes it to Docker Hub, and applies the manifests to your cluster. 2. **Docker Hub** → `zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest` image appears. 3. **Kubernetes** → Two pods running, service exposed (check with `kubectl get svc`). --- ### What if you can’t push? If you’re running this in an environment that can’t access the internet or GitHub, just copy the file contents above into the appropriate files locally. Once you have network access, run the `git add/commit/push` commands. Happy coding! 🚀
